---
title: "Comparing Univariate ANOVA and MANOVA for Hypothesis Testing in Cyclic Data Settings"
author: "Christie Ngo"
format: typst
editor: visual

# Introduction

Real world data is rarely perfectly normally distributed. Though many statistical models require assumptions to hold true for inference, there is still valuable information extracted from imperfect data. Especially in nature, patterns often surface when considering biological and seasonal phenomena. Data extracted ranging the angular velocity of zebrafish in circular wells or heart rhythm monitoring can lead to predictable cycles.

When observations within a single population follow a trend, independence is violated and there is an inflated type one error rate along with biased p-values. To understand how cyclic data can influence Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA), 3-dimensional data is simulated for two distinct populations in R. For the first question, we test if violations to the independence assumption of cyclic data can still detect a true difference in population means. Our second question of interest pertains to whether the same mean vectors will register as so when we add sufficient noise to negate the cyclic dependency. In both scenarios, we compare the results between the MANOVA output with the majority hypothesis decision for the univariate ANOVA tests, corrected using Bonferroni for multiple testing.

Findings indicate that 



# Method

MANOVA is a model for comparison of multivariate mean vectors. The observation vector takes the form:

$$\mathbf{X}_{lj} = \mathbf{\mu} + \mathbf{\tau}_l + \mathbf{e}_{lj}$$ $l$ is the number of observations in each group whereas $j$ represents the number of groups. Each component in $\mathbf{X}_{lj}$ satisfies the univariate ANOVA model. $\mathbf{\mu}$ is the overall mean while $\mathbf{\tau}_{l}$ is the treatment effect of the $l^{th}$ treatment subject to the constraint $\sum^g_{l=1} n_l\tau_l = 0$ for identifiability. $\mathbf{e}_{lj}$ are errors represented by independent variables of distribution $N_p(0, \Sigma)$.

## Assumptions

- Both populations are distributed as multivariate normal (univariate normal for ANOVA).

- Observations are randomly sampled from their respective population and independent within and between groups.

- The two groups share a common variance ($\Sigma$ matrix in MANOVA).

## Hypothesis Testing

We let the baseline population be $1$ and the modified population be $2$. Our testing is as followed:

ANOVA (for each of the dimensions):

$H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$

$H_a: \mu_1 \neq \mu_2$

MANOVA:

$H_0: \vec{\mu}_1 = \vec{\mu}_2$

$H_a: \vec{\mu}_1 \neq \vec{\mu}_2$

## Multiple Testing Correction

To account for the repeated univariate tests, we apply the Bonferroni correction by dividing our $alpha = 0.05$ value by the number of tests ($3$). Because increasing the number of tests allows for more opportunity to obtain a significant result due to chance, we account for this by using a more conservative p-value threshold.

## Simulations

In both generated datasets, we create two populations with three dimensions and $200$ observations. The independent vector $x$ consists of 200 points equally spaced across $32\pi$ or 16 rotations (with the addition of some normally distributed noise centered at 0 with a low standard deviation of 0.1). The dependent vectors $Y1$, $Y2$, and $Y3$ use the sine of $x$ function, the cosine of $x$ function, and sine of $2x$ function, respectively. Without any modifications, the mean value of each function should be symmetric about and thus have an expected value of 0.

#### Cyclic Dependency

To visually assess the strength of the cyclic relationship, we use the Autocorrelation Function (ACF) plot. At each lag, or data at a set point a past time, we are able to determine its correlation with the series. Repeating peaks at predictable time intervals indicate seasonality.

#### True difference in means

We want to maintain the cyclic structure, so we add a small amount of normally distributed noise but with a slightly shifted mean of 0.12. The differences are apparent in the lack of overlap between the populations in @partone3d. Using the @acfone plot below, we can confirm that there is still seasonality in our generated dataset.

```{r}
library(mvtnorm)
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(15)

alpha = 0.05
r = 1000
n = 200
reject_match = 0
fail_match = 0
y1_capture = 0
y2_capture = 0
y3_capture = 0
manova_reject = 0
anova_reject = 0

for (i in 1:r){
  x <- seq(0, 32 * pi, length.out = n)+rnorm(200, sd=0.1)
  y_11 <- sin(x)+rnorm(200, sd=0.1)
  y_12 <- cos(x)+rnorm(200, sd=0.1)
  y_13 <- sin(2*x)+rnorm(200, sd=0.1)
  X1 <- cbind(x, y_11, y_12, y_13)
  
  
  y_21 <- sin(x)+rnorm(200, mean=0.12, sd=0.1)
  y_22 <- cos(x)+rnorm(200, mean=0.12, sd=0.1)
  y_23 <- sin(2*x)+rnorm(200, mean=0.12, sd=0.1)
  X2 <- cbind(x, y_21, y_22, y_23)
  
  
  dat <- as.data.frame(rbind(X1, X2)) |>
    mutate(group = factor(rep(c(1, 2), each = n)))

  colnames(dat) <- c("X", "Y1", "Y2", "Y3", "group")
  
  manova_res <- manova(cbind(Y1, Y2, Y3) ~ group, data = dat)
  out_summary <- summary(manova_res, test = "Wilks")

  manova_p_value = out_summary$stats[, "Pr(>F)"][[1]]
  
  y1_test = t.test(X1[, 2], X2[, 2], var.equal = TRUE)
  y1_pvalue = y1_test$p.value
  if (y1_test$conf[[1]] <= -0.12 && y1_test$conf[[2]] >= -0.12){
    y1_capture = y1_capture + 1
  }
  
  y2_test = t.test(X1[, 3], X2[, 3], var.equal = TRUE)
  y2_pvalue = y2_test$p.value
  if (y2_test$conf[[1]] <= -0.12 && y2_test$conf[[2]] >= -0.12){
    y2_capture = y2_capture + 1
  }
  
  y3_test = t.test(X1[, 4], X2[, 4], var.equal = TRUE)
  y3_pvalue = y3_test$p.value

  if (y3_test$conf[[1]] <= -0.12 && y3_test$conf[[2]] >= -0.12){
    y3_capture = y3_capture + 1
  }

  count = 0
  if (manova_p_value <= alpha){
    manova_reject = manova_reject+1
    if (y1_pvalue <= alpha/3){
      count = count + 1
    }
    if (y2_pvalue <= alpha/3){
      count = count + 1
    }
    if (y3_pvalue <= alpha/3){
      count = count + 1
    }
    
    if (count >= 2){
      reject_match = reject_match + 1
      anova_reject = anova_reject + 1
    }
  }
  
  else{
    if (y1_pvalue > alpha/3){
      count = count + 1
    }
    if (y2_pvalue > alpha/3){
      count = count + 1
    }
    if (y3_pvalue > alpha/3){
      count = count + 1
    }
    
    if (count >= 2){
      fail_match = fail_match + 1
    } else{ anova_reject = anova_reject + 1 }
  }
    
  }

paste0("Proportion of matching results: ", (fail_match+reject_match)/1000)
test1_matching = (fail_match+reject_match)/1000

paste0("Proportion of matching fail to reject: ", (fail_match)/1000)
test1_matching_fail = fail_match/1000

paste0("Proportion of matching reject: ", (reject_match)/1000)
test1_matching_reject = reject_match/1000

paste0("Proportion of MANOVA reject: ", (manova_reject)/1000)
test1_manova_reject = manova_reject/1000

paste0("Proportion of ANOVA majority reject: ", (anova_reject)/1000)
test1_anova_reject = anova_reject/1000

paste0("Proportion of mismatched results: ", (1000-fail_match+reject_match)/1000)
test1_mismatched = (1000-fail_match+reject_match)/1000

paste0("Proportion of True Y1 Value: ", (y1_capture)/1000)
test1_y1_true = y1_capture/1000

paste0("Proportion of True Y2 Value: ", (y2_capture)/1000)
test1_y2_true = y2_capture/1000

paste0("Proportion of True Y3 Value: ", (y3_capture)/1000)
test1_y3_true = y3_capture/1000


fit <- lm(
  cbind(Y1, Y2, Y3) ~ X + group,
  data = dat
)

E <- residuals(fit)
```

```{r partone3d, fig.cap="3D Scatterplot of True Difference In Cyclic Means", warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
library(plotly)

plot_ly(data = dat, 
        x = ~Y1, 
        y = ~Y2, 
        z = ~Y3, 
        color = ~group,          
        colors = c("#B10DC9", "#85144b"),
        type = "scatter3d", 
        mode = "markers")
```

```{r acfone, fig.cap="ACF Plot of Each Dimension's Residuals for True Difference In Cyclic Means", warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
par(mfrow = c(3, 1))

acf(E[, "Y1"], main = "ACF of y1 residuals")
acf(E[, "Y2"], main = "ACF of y2 residuals")
acf(E[, "Y3"], main = "ACF of y3 residuals")
```

#### Independence from cyclic data

For our second simulation, we want to see if adding sufficient noise to effectively reduce dependence between points in the cycle will lead to hypothesis tests detecting significant differences between populations, despite them being identically distributed. We ended up with adding normal errors with a standard deviation before the independence assumption held. In the @parttwo3d plot, we can see that the noise now makes the populations appear indistinguishable, which is promising given their identical distributions. Again, we examine the ACF plot (@acftwo) to confirm there is no longer a trend within the lags.

```{r}
library(mvtnorm)
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(15)
alpha = 0.05
r = 1000
n = 200
reject_match = 0
fail_match = 0
y1_capture = 0
y2_capture = 0
y3_capture = 0
manova_failreject = 0
anova_failreject = 0

for (i in 1:r){
  x <- seq(0, 32 * pi, length.out = n)+rnorm(200, sd=1)
  y_11 <- sin(x)+rnorm(200, sd=1)
  y_12 <- cos(x)+rnorm(200, sd=1)
  y_13 <- sin(2*x)+rnorm(200, sd=1)
  X1 <- cbind(x, y_11, y_12, y_13)
  
  
  y_21 <- sin(x)+rnorm(200, sd=1)
  y_22 <- cos(x)+rnorm(200, sd=1)
  y_23 <- sin(2*x)+rnorm(200, sd=1)
  X2 <- cbind(x, y_21, y_22, y_23)
  
  
  dat <- as.data.frame(rbind(X1, X2)) |>
    mutate(group = factor(rep(c(1, 2), each = n)))

  colnames(dat) <- c("X", "Y1", "Y2", "Y3", "group")
  
  manova_res <- manova(cbind(Y1, Y2, Y3) ~ group, data = dat)
  out_summary <- summary(manova_res, test = "Wilks")

  manova_p_value = out_summary$stats[, "Pr(>F)"][[1]]
  
  y1_test = t.test(X1[, 2], X2[, 2], var.equal = TRUE)
  y1_pvalue = y1_test$p.value
  if (y1_test$conf[[1]] <= 0 && y1_test$conf[[2]] >= 0){
    y1_capture = y1_capture + 1
  }
  
  y2_test = t.test(X1[, 3], X2[, 3], var.equal = TRUE)
  y2_pvalue = y2_test$p.value
  if (y2_test$conf[[1]] <= 0 && y2_test$conf[[2]] >= 0){
    y2_capture = y2_capture + 1
  }
  
  y3_test = t.test(X1[, 4], X2[, 4], var.equal = TRUE)
  y3_pvalue = y3_test$p.value

  if (y3_test$conf[[1]] <= 0 && y3_test$conf[[2]] >= 0){
    y3_capture = y3_capture + 1
  }

  count = 0

  if (manova_p_value <= alpha){
    if (y1_pvalue <= alpha/3){
      count = count + 1
    }
    if (y2_pvalue <= alpha/3){
      count = count + 1
    }
    if (y3_pvalue <= alpha/3){
      count = count + 1
    }
    
    if (count >= 2){
      reject_match = reject_match + 1
    } else { anova_failreject = anova_failreject + 1 }
  }
  
  else{
    manova_failreject = manova_failreject+1
    if (y1_pvalue > alpha/3){
      count = count + 1
    }
    if (y2_pvalue > alpha/3){
      count = count + 1
    }
    if (y3_pvalue > alpha/3){
      count = count + 1
    }
    
    if (count >= 2){
      fail_match = fail_match + 1
      anova_failreject = anova_failreject+1
    }
  }
    
  }


paste0("Proportion of matching results: ", (fail_match+reject_match)/1000)
test2_matching = (fail_match+reject_match)/1000

paste0("Proportion of matching fail to reject: ", (fail_match)/1000)
test2_matching_fail = fail_match/1000

paste0("Proportion of MANOVA fail to reject: ", (manova_failreject)/1000)
test2_manova_fail = manova_failreject/1000

paste0("Proportion of ANOVA majority fail to reject: ", (anova_failreject)/1000)
test2_anova_fail = anova_failreject/1000

paste0("Proportion of matching reject: ", (reject_match)/1000)
test2_matching_reject = reject_match/1000

paste0("Proportion of mismatched results: ", (1000-fail_match+reject_match)/1000)
test2_mismatched = (1000-fail_match+reject_match)/1000

paste0("Proportion of True Y1 Value: ", (y1_capture)/1000)
test2_y1_true = y1_capture/1000

paste0("Proportion of True Y2 Value: ", (y2_capture)/1000)
test2_y2_true = y2_capture/1000

paste0("Proportion of True Y3 Value: ", (y3_capture)/1000)
test2_y3_true = y3_capture/1000


fit <- lm(
  cbind(Y1, Y2, Y3) ~ X + group,
  data = dat
)

E <- residuals(fit)
```

```{r parttwo3d, fig.cap="3D Scatterplot of Independence from Cyclic Data", warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
library(plotly)

plot_ly(data = dat, 
        x = ~Y1, 
        y = ~Y2, 
        z = ~Y3, 
        color = ~group,          
        colors = c("#0057B8", "#007A73"),
        type = "scatter3d", 
        mode = "markers")
```

```{r acftwo, fig.cap="ACF Plot of Each Dimension's Residuals for Independence from Cyclic Data", echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
par(mfrow = c(3, 1))

acf(E[, "Y1"], main = "ACF of y1 residuals")
acf(E[, "Y2"], main = "ACF of y2 residuals")
acf(E[, "Y3"], main = "ACF of y3 residuals")
```

# Results

When considering the aggregated outcomes of 1000 trials for each research setting, there was neither MANOVA nor ANOVA outperformed the other in entirety. In the first experiment involving a true difference in means with an independence violation, MANOVA undoubtedly returned better results. Although each univariate ANOVA successfully captured the true difference in means parameter for each dimension in all of the trials, the majority decision never rejected the null hypothesis. On the other hand, MANOVA acknowledged the true difference in means for 76% of the trials. In this case, MANOVA is more promising for detecting a small population difference within cyclic data.

For the second experiment with achieving independence from same distribution cyclic data, the results of both methods were comparable. In this setting, ANOVA confidence intervals for the true difference in means contained the true parameter roughly 98% of the time, instead of 100% as it was previously. ANOVA failed to reject the null hypothesis in every trial while MANOVA failed to reject 99.3% of the time. Since the added normal noise had a sizable standard deviation and the population scatterplots are entirely overlapped, it is expected that both methods were able to easily detect no difference in means.
